claim: Cells change their volume depending on the rate at which they change shape when they spontaneously spread or when they are externally deformed.
source: We found that cells change their volume depending on the rate at which they change shape, when they spontaneously spread or when they are externally deformed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cells undergo slow deformation at constant volume, while fast deformation leads to volume loss.
source: Cells undergo slow deformation at constant volume, while fast deformation leads to volume loss.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Volume modulation depends on the state of the actin cortex and the coupling of ion fluxes to membrane tension.
source: Our model and experiments suggest that volume modulation depends on the state of the actin cortex and the coupling of ion fluxes to membrane tension.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with actin-disrupting drugs and ion channel inhibitors in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Migrating cells can undergo large deformations in a variety of physiological and pathological contexts.
source: In recent years, in vivo imaging has revealed that, in a variety of physiological and pathological contexts, cells undergo large deformations (Weigelin et al., 2014), sometimes being squeezed to a tenth of their resting diameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fast-moving immune or cancer cells can deform to a large extent in only a few minutes.
source: Migrating cells, in particular fast-moving immune or cancer cells, can deform to a large extent in only a few minutes (Thiam et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2017; Beunk et al., 2019), for example, when they cross an endothelial barrier (Subramanian et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Circulating cells can undergo deformations below the second timescale when pushed through small blood capillaries.
source: Even faster deformations, below the second timescale, can be observed in circulating cells pushed through small blood capillaries.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cell deformation in circulation.

claim: Large cell deformations are physiological and occur across a large range of timescales.
source: Altogether, these examples show that large cell deformations are physiological and occur across a large range of timescales.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the examples provided in the preceding sentences.

claim: Large cell shape changes must involve significant changes in volume, surface area, or both.
source: Large cell shape changes must involve significant changes in volume, surface area, or both.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on geometric principles.

claim: The number of studies on cell volume modulation upon cell deformation is still very small.
source: But the number of studies on cell volume modulation upon cell deformation is still very small (Guilak, 1995; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the literature, with citations to a few existing studies.

claim: It is not clear whether cells behave as poroelastic materials losing volume when pressed, or like liquid droplets extending surface area at constant volume.
source: It is still not clear whether the material that cells are made of is rather poroelastic (Moeendarbary et al., 2013), losing volume when pressed, or behaves like a liquid droplet, extending its surface area at constant volume.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field, with a citation to work on poroelasticity.

claim: Two articles measuring volume using 3D reconstruction from confocal slices report that cells that are more spread are smaller in volume.
source: Two articles, measuring volume using 3D reconstruction from confocal slices, report that cells that are more spread are smaller in volume (Guo et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2018), leading to a higher density and potential long-term effects on cell fate (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Another article using volume measurements by fluorescence exclusion reports no or slightly positive correlation between spreading area and cell volume.
source: On the other hand, another article, using volume measurements by fluorescence exclusion (FXm), reports no or slightly positive correlation between spreading area and cell volume (Perez Gonzalez et al., 2018), reflecting the fact that as cells grow larger, their spreading area also increases.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Different models have been proposed to explain a coupling between cell shape changes and cell volume modulation.
source: Different models have recently been proposed to explain a coupling between cells shape changes and cell volume modulation (Guo et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2018; Adar and Safran, 2020; McEvoy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple modeling studies.

claim: Most models are based on the scenario that cell shape changes can stress the cell surface, including the membrane and the actin cortex.
source: Most of them are based on the same type of scenario: depending on the timescale and extent of the deformation, cell shape changes can stress the cell surface, including the membrane and the actin cortex (Chugh and Paluch, 2018).
evidence: This claim summarizes the common basis of existing models, with a citation.

claim: Stress in cell surface structures can be relaxed due to cortex turnover, unfolding of membrane reservoirs, and detachment of the membrane from the cortex with the formation of blebs.
source: This stress can be relaxed due to cortex turnover, unfolding of membrane reservoirs (Pietuch and Janshoff, 2013), and detachment of the membrane from the cortex with the formation of blebs (Tinevez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on stress relaxation mechanisms.

claim: Stress in cell surface structures can lead to the modulation of ion fluxes resulting in cell volume changes.
source: Stress in these structures can also lead to the modulation of ion fluxes (Jiang and Sun, 2013) resulting in cell volume changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The consequences of the mechano-osmotic coupling scenario have not been explored in depth experimentally.
source: Despite its broad relevance for cell mechanics and cell physiology, the consequences of this type of scenario have not been explored in depth experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: When cells deform as they spread on a flat adhesive surface, the degree of volume changes depends on the speed of spreading.
source: Using FXm to accurately measure volume in live cells (Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015; Cadart et al., 2017; Cadart et al., 2018), we found that when cells deform as they spread on a flat adhesive surface, the degree of volume changes depends on the speed of spreading.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The authors propose an extension of the classical pump and leak model including a mechano-osmotic coupling activated upon cell deformation occurring faster than the membrane tension/actin cortex relaxation timescale.
source: To explain this observation, we propose an extension of the classical pump and leak model (PLM; Cadart et al., 2019), including a mechano-osmotic coupling activated upon cell deformation occurring faster than the membrane tension/actin cortex relaxation timescale.
evidence: This is the main theoretical contribution of the study, described in the abstract and developed in the Results section.

claim: In a population growing and dividing at steady state, HeLa cells expressing hGeminin-mCherry do not display a strong correlation between their spreading area and their volume.
source: We did not find any strong correlation between spreading area and volume for HeLa hGeminin-mCherry, as well as for HeLa EMBL (Kyoto) and RPE-1 cells measuring their spreading area with reflection interference contrast microscopy (RICM) (Rädler and Sackmann, 1993; Cuvelier et al., 2007), larger cells in volume being also slightly more spread (Figure 1A graph and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: A clearer positive correlation between volume and spreading area was observed for 3T3 fibroblasts.
source: A clearer positive correlation was observed for 3T3 fibroblasts, which were also generally more spread for a given volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S/G2 cells tend to be larger and more spread than G1 cells.
source: Using the hGeminin cell cycle marker, we observed that S/G2 cells tend to be larger and more spread than G1 cells (Figure 1A graph), suggesting that the positive correlation is simply due to cell growth, with cells increasing their spreading area as they grow.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using the hGeminin cell cycle marker.

claim: There is no correlation between cell volume and spreading area at any given cell cycle stage.
source: Considering the same group of cells at various times after mitosis, or after the G1/S transition, we could not observe any correlation between cell volume and spreading area at any given cell cycle stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A for cells at specific cell cycle stages.

claim: The distribution of volumes did not change when cells were plated on smaller adhesive patterns.
source: We found that the distribution of volumes did not change when cells were plated on smaller adhesive patterns (Figure 1B graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B for cells on micropatterns.

claim: There is no strong correlation, at the cell population level, between spreading area and cell volume, independently of the cell cycle stage.
source: Overall, these experiments suggest that, as reported before (Perez Gonzalez et al., 2018), there is no strong correlation, at the cell population level, between spreading area and cell volume, independently of the cell cycle stage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments in Figure 1, with a citation to a previous study.

claim: When plated on a fibronectin-coated substrate, HeLa EMBL cells showed a transition from a sphere to a half-sphere in about 15 min, then continued spreading by extending lamellipodial protrusions.
source: When plated on a fibronectin-coated substrate, HeLa EMBL cells showed a transition from a sphere to a half-sphere in about 15 min, then continued spreading by extending lamellipodial protrusions (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C and video 1.

claim: Cell spreading was accompanied by a small (5% on average) but significant loss of volume, typically occurring during the first 20 min of spreading and followed by a volume increase of about 5%/hr.
source: Cell spreading was accompanied by a small (5% on average) but significant loss of volume, typically occurring during the first 20 min of spreading and followed by a volume increase of about 5%/hr, in the range of the expected cell growth for a doubling time of about 20 hr (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E, F, and G.

claim: The absolute precision of volume measurements is within 10%, evaluated by comparing the initial average volume of cell populations in different chambers and on different days.
source: The absolute precision of our measurements is within 10%, evaluated by comparing the initial average volume of cell populations in different chambers and on different days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim describes the precision of the measurement method, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The accuracy of the measurement when following the same individual cell is rather 1%.
source: But the accuracy of the measurement when following the same individual cell is rather 1% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, evaluated by measuring the volume of the same cell multiple times at a 30 ms frame rate).
evidence: This claim describes the accuracy of the measurement method, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Only cell volume decreased while dry mass remained constant over the few tens of minutes of initial cell spreading.
source: Combining quantitative phase and volume measurement, we found that only cell volume decreased while dry mass remained constant over the few tens of minutes of initial cell spreading (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), causing a transient density increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data combining volume and dry mass measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The volume loss during spreading suggests a loss of water (and probably small osmolites like ions) from the cell, similar to volume regulatory decrease following a hypo-osmotic shock.
source: This suggests a loss of water (and probably small osmolites like ions) from the cell, similar to volume regulatory decrease following a hypo-osmotic shock (Pedersen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that volume decreases while dry mass remains constant, with a citation to work on volume regulation.

claim: Cells plated on PLL-PEG, instead of fibronectin, did not spread and displayed an increase in the volume of about 7%/hr.
source: Cells plated on PLL-PEG, instead of fibronectin, did not spread and displayed an increase in the volume of about 7%/hr (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E for cells on PLL-PEG.

claim: The spreading dynamics rather than the final spreading area might be coupled to the loss of volume.
source: This result, together with our observation on steady-state spread cells, suggests that the spreading dynamics rather than the final spreading area might be coupled to the loss of volume.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of spreading cells and steady-state cells.

claim: Faster-spreading cells lose more volume, whereas slow-spreading cells lose less volume or do not lose volume at all.
source: Pooling cells together according to their spreading speed, we observed that faster-spreading cells were losing more volume, whereas slow-spreading cells lost less volume or did not lose volume at all (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H for cells grouped by spreading speed.

claim: Faster spreading cells also lose volume faster in the initial spreading phase.
source: The graph clearly shows that faster spreading cells also lose volume faster in this initial spreading phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1I plotting spreading speed against volume loss rate.

claim: Spreading speed and volume loss are both slowing down with time.
source: Spreading speed and volume loss are both slowing down with time (Figure 1J), whereas absolute spreading area increases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The amount of volume lost was not correlated with the initial cell volume.
source: Conversely, the amount of volume lost was not correlated with the initial cell volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Volume loss in spreading cells is a transient phenomenon correlated with the spreading kinetics and not the absolute spreading area.
source: Overall, these data show that volume loss in spreading cells is a transient phenomenon correlated with the spreading kinetics and not the absolute spreading area.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments in Figure 1.

claim: Early spreading dynamics were shown to strongly depend on the properties of the actomyosin cortex.
source: Early spreading dynamics were shown to strongly depend on the properties of the actomyosin cortex (Cuvelier et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Lat A-treated cells spread slower than control cells.
source: As expected, we found that Lat A-treated cells spread slower, while Y-27-treated cells spread faster than control cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Y-27-treated cells spread faster than control cells.
source: As expected, we found that Lat A-treated cells spread slower, while Y-27-treated cells spread faster than control cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lat A treated cells lost less volume (2–3%) than control cells.
source: Accordingly, Lat A treated cells lost less volume (2–3%) than control cells, while Y-27 treated cells lost more (10–15%, Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Y-27 treated cells lost more volume (10–15%) than control cells.
source: Accordingly, Lat A treated cells lost less volume (2–3%) than control cells, while Y-27 treated cells lost more (10–15%, Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Y-27 treated cells plated on PLL-PEG substrate on which they could not spread, increased their volume like control cells.
source: Y-27 treated cells plated on PLL-PEG substrate on which they could not spread, increased their volume like control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), thereby showing that larger volume loss was not due to the drug treatment itself but was a result of the spreading kinetics in the presence of the drug.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The coupling between spreading speed and volume loss was found to be very similar for other cell types, RPE-1 and 3T3.
source: This coupling between spreading speed and volume loss was also found to be very similar for other cell types, RPE-1 and 3T3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-I), although RPE-1 cells displayed an initial phase of volume increase before eventually losing volume (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F, H, I), a phenomenon that we have not investigated further in this article.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-I.

claim: RPE-1 cells displayed an initial phase of volume increase before eventually losing volume.
source: This coupling between spreading speed and volume loss was also found to be very similar for other cell types, RPE-1 and 3T3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-I), although RPE-1 cells displayed an initial phase of volume increase before eventually losing volume (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F, H, I), a phenomenon that we have not investigated further in this article.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F, H, I.

claim: The initial phase of volume increase in RPE-1 cells was lost upon Y-27 treatment.
source: This initial phase of volume increase was lost upon Y-27 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that it was due to induction of contractility through mechanotransduction pathways (Burridge et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and I, with a citation to work on mechanotransduction.

claim: Adding 1 mM MnCl2 during the spreading experiment increased spreading speed and also increased the volume loss.
source: In order to increase spreading speed without changing cell contractility, we added 1 mM MnCl2 during the spreading experiment. This treatment increased spreading speed, as previously reported (Edwards et al., 1988) and also increased the volume loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and Figure 2D, with a citation to previous work on MnCl2 effects.

claim: A general effect of spreading speed on volume modulation exists, with a loss of volume reaching up to 20% for fast-spreading cells.
source: These data together suggest a general effect of spreading speed on volume modulation, with a loss of volume reaching up to 20% for fast-spreading cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments with various drug treatments.

claim: Volume loss exceeding 1% is considered to be dominated by osmotic volume regulation.
source: Water loss exceeding 1% is considered to be dominated by osmotic volume regulation (see Appendix 1 and Cadart et al., 2019; Yellin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and the appendix.

claim: Volume set point and large volume modulation such as volume regulatory response following osmotic shocks can be accounted for by the general theoretical framework of the PLM.
source: Volume set point and large volume modulation such as volume regulatory response following osmotic shocks can be accounted for by the general theoretical framework of the PLM (see Appendix 1 and Cadart et al., 2019; Tosteson and Hoffman, 1960; Kay, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on the pump and leak model.

claim: The cell volume is determined by an osmotic balance involving the active pumping of specific ions (mainly sodium and potassium) to compensate for the pressure from impermeant solutes in the cell.
source: Briefly, the cell volume is determined by an osmotic balance involving the active pumping of specific ions (mainly sodium and potassium) to compensate for the pressure from impermeant solutes in the cell (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the pump and leak model, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells showed the expected response to both hypo and hyperosmotic shocks, with a fast change in volume (less than a minute timescale) followed by a slower adaptation (timescale of minutes).
source: Cells showed the expected response to both hypo and hyperosmotic shocks, with a fast change in volume (less than a minute timescale) followed by a slower adaptation (timescale of minutes) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Fast changes in volume upon osmotic shock were not accompanied by any change in dry mass and thus corresponded to water (and ion) fluxes.
source: We also checked, using quantitative phase measure of dry mass, that these fast changes in volume were not accompanied by any change in dry mass and thus corresponded to water (and ion) fluxes, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Ponder relation showed a very good agreement with previous reports, with a linear relation between the change in volume and the change in osmotic pressure, over a large range of imposed external osmolality.
source: Ponder's plot showed a very good agreement with previous reports (Pritchard and Guilak, 2004; Zhou et al., 2009), with a linear relation between the change in volume and the change in osmotic pressure, over a large range of imposed external osmolality (Figure 3D) and corresponds to about 30% of osmotically inactive volume (volume occupied by large molecules or solid components).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, with citations to previous work.

claim: The Ponder relation does not depend on the integrity of the actin cytoskeleton, as cells treated with 2 µM Lat A show the same relation.
source: As shown by others (Pritchard and Guilak, 2004), we find that the Ponder relation does not depend on the integrity of the actin cytoskeleton, as cells treated with 2 µM Lat A show the same relation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Ponder relation does not depend on the inhibition of sodium/proton exchanger NHE1 by 50 µm EIPA.
source: Ponder relation does not depend either on the inhibition of sodium/proton exchanger NHE1 by 50 µm EIPA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cell volume measurements are accurate, even for small volume changes, and cells display the expected response to osmotic shocks, explained by the classical PLM.
source: These results show both that our cell volume measurements are accurate, even for small volume changes, and that our cells display the expected response to osmotic shocks, explained by the classical PLM, in agreement with previously published results (Ponder and Saslow, 1931; Pritchard and Guilak, 2004; Zhou et al., 2009; Roffay et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the osmotic shock experiments, with citations to previous work.

claim: Cells treated with Y-27, which spread faster than control cells, displayed a higher tether force during the spreading phase, while the force was similar to control cells at steady state.
source: We found that cells treated with Y-27, which spread faster than control cells, displayed a higher tether force during the spreading phase, while the force was similar to control cells at steady state (Figure 3E), showing that the increase was not due to the drug treatment itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cells that stayed rounded because they had been plated on small (20 µm in diameter) micropatterns, measured 4–5 hr after seeding, had a low membrane tension, treated or not with Y-27632.
source: Importantly, we also showed that cells that stayed rounded because they had been plated on small (20 µm in diameter) micropatterns, measured 4–5 hr after seeding, had a low membrane tension, treated or not with Y-27632.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The experiment suggests an effect of spreading speed on membrane tension.
source: This experiment suggests an effect of spreading speed on membrane tension.
evidence: This is an inference from the tether pulling experiments.

claim: Membrane tension might modulate cell volume upon fast cell shape changes.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that membrane tension might modulate cell volume upon fast cell shape changes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the tether pulling experiments.

claim: The change of volume occurred in a timescale of seconds upon osmotic shock.
source: The change of volume occurred in a timescale of seconds, as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The permeability appeared smaller for hyper-osmotic shocks than for hypo-osmotic shocks.
source: This allowed us to estimate the permeability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which appeared smaller for hyper-osmotic shocks than for hypo-osmotic shocks, as reported previously (Chara et al., 2005; Peckys et al., 2011), although the reason for this difference is not understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to previous work.

claim: Volume adapted faster for larger osmotic shocks.
source: It showed that volume adapted faster for larger shocks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The response to osmotic shock was quite homogenous for the recovery from hypertonic shocks, while there was a higher cell-cell variability during recovery from hypotonic shocks.
source: At the level of individual cells, the response was quite homogenous for the recovery from hypertonic shocks, while there was a higher cell-cell variability during recovery from hypotonic shocks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), with cells showing only partial recovery, especially for large hypo-osmotic shocks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The rate of volume change observed for small osmotic shocks is similar to the rate of volume change during cell spreading experiments (about 10 μm3/min).
source: Importantly, the rate of volume change observed for small shocks is similar to the rate of volume change during cell spreading experiments (about 10 μm3/min).
evidence: This is a comparison of rates from different experiments.

claim: The use of a mechanosensitive PLM to explain the cell spreading data is justified by the similarity of timescales.
source: This justifies the use of a mechanosensitive PLM to explain the cell spreading data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of timescales.

claim: In the mechanosensitive PLM model, the dependence of the volume on membrane tension is through the mechanosensitivity of the ion channels and pumps.
source: In brief, in this new model (see details in Appendix 1), the dependence of the volume on membrane tension is through the mechanosensitivity of the ion channels and pumps.
evidence: This is a description of the model proposed by the authors.

claim: If the mechanosensitivity parameter is negative, then the volume will decrease upon an increase in the tension.
source: If the mechanosensitivity parameter is negative, then the volume will decrease upon an increase in the tension.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: For physiological values of parameters found in the literature, the mechanosensitivity parameter is expected to be negative.
source: For physiological values of parameters found in the literature (see values in Appendix 1), we expect to be negative.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model based on literature values.

claim: The mechanosensitive PLM predicts the observed proportionality between volume loss and the speed of spreading, and no dependency on the absolute cell spreading area.
source: Importantly, this simple extension of the PLM predicts the observed proportionality between volume loss and the speed of spreading, and no dependency on the absolute cell spreading area (Equation 3, Figures 1I, 2C and D).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that matches the experimental observations.

claim: The mechanosensitive PLM model allowed a satisfactory fit of the experimental volume data.
source: The spreading parameters were extracted from the experimental spreading data, and the model allowed a satisfactory fit of the experimental volume data (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model fits shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells have a very large excess of membrane surface area, with the plasma membrane rupturing when cells reached 5.7 times their initial volume.
source: We found that on average, the plasma membrane ruptured when cells reached 5.7 times their initial volume, which corresponds to an excess of membrane surface area of about 3.3 times, in accordance with previous measures (Ting-Beall et al., 1993; Guilak et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, with citations to previous work.

claim: Cells have a very large excess of membrane surface area and membrane tension could not arise from a limitation in the total amount of membrane.
source: It means that cells have a very large excess of membrane surface area and that membrane tension could not arise from a limitation in the total amount of membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the membrane rupture experiments.

claim: The plasma membrane being bound to the underlying cytoskeleton, its restricted unfolding could generate an increase in tension depending on the rate of cell deformation.
source: Nevertheless, the plasma membrane being bound to the underlying cytoskeleton, its restricted unfolding could generate an increase in tension depending on the rate of cell deformation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain how tension could increase despite excess membrane.

claim: CK-666 treatment alone induced both a slower spreading and lower volume loss (2–3%).
source: We found that CK-666 treatment alone induced both a slower spreading and lower volume loss (2–3%, Figure 5A and B), similar to the low Lat A treatment (Figure 2B and C), which was well fitted by the mechanosensitive PLM (fits on Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Treatment with Y-27 increased the spreading speed of CK-666 treated cells, but the volume did not decrease in this fast-spreading condition.
source: Treatment with Y-27 increased the spreading speed of CK-666 treated cells, but the volume did not decrease in this fast-spreading condition (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Inhibition of Piezo and NHE1 did not affect the initial average cell volume.
source: By contrast, inhibition of these two channels did not affect the initial average cell volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with GdCl3 led to an increase in volume loss (from 5% to 8%), which could be fully accounted for by the increase in cell spreading speed.
source: Treatment with GdCl3 led to an increase in volume loss (from 5% to 8%), which could be fully accounted for by the increase in cell spreading speed (Figure 5E and F) and well fitted by the mechanosensitive PLM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: HeLa EMBL cells treated with EIPA, while spreading slightly faster than control cells, lost less volume.
source: On the other hand, HeLa EMBL cells treated with EIPA, while spreading slightly faster than control cells, lost less volume (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Combining EIPA with Y-27 showed that, despite a fast spreading speed comparable to Y-27 treated cells, NHE1 inhibition fully prevented volume loss during fast spreading.
source: Combining EIPA with Y-27 showed that, despite a fast spreading speed comparable to Y-27 treated cells, NHE1 inhibition fully prevented volume loss (Figure 5G and H), an effect that we also observed for RPE-1 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: None of the drug treatments performed significantly affected the initial volume of cells prior to spreading.
source: Importantly none of the drug treatments performed significantly affected the initial volume of cells prior to spreading (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mechanosensitive PLM predicts that inhibition of the mechano-osmotic coupling in fast-spreading cells would prevent the associated volume loss and lead to an increase in the membrane tension during the spreading phase.
source: The mechanosensitive PLM predicts that inhibition of the mechano-osmotic coupling in fast-spreading cells, would prevent the associated volume loss, and lead to an increase in the membrane tension during the spreading phase.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Disrupting the mechano-osmotic coupling in fast-spreading cells (Y-27 plus CK-666 or Y-27 plus EIPA) leads to the highest tether force values in the spreading phase, while the steady-state values did not change.
source: These experiments showed that, as predicted by the model, disrupting the mechano-osmotic coupling in fast-spreading cells (Y-27 plus CK-666 or Y-27 plus EIPA) leads to the highest tether force values in the spreading phase, while the steady-state values did not change.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Tension was highest during early spreading compared to steady-state spread cells, suggesting that the increase was due to spreading and not to the drug treatments alone.
source: Tension was highest during early spreading compared to steady-state spread cells, suggesting that the increase was due to spreading and not to the drug treatments alone, even though EIPA alone also add an effect on steady-state tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: In cells where the coupling between membrane tension and volume regulation is lost, fast spreading in the absence of volume loss induces higher tension increase.
source: This shows that, in these cells, the coupling between membrane tension and volume regulation is lost, and that fast spreading in the absence of volume loss induces higher tension increase (Figure 5J and K), as predicted by the model (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and K, and model predictions in Figure 5I.

claim: The experiments confirm the validity of the mechanosensitive PLM.
source: Taken together, these experiments confirm the validity of our mechanosensitive PLM.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments testing the model predictions.

claim: The experiments support the existence of a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism that reduces the extent of changes in membrane tension upon fast cell shape changes by modulating the relative contribution of surface expansion and volume loss.
source: They also support the existence of a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism that reduces the extent of changes in membrane tension upon fast cell shape changes by modulating the relative contribution of surface expansion and volume loss.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments and model.

claim: While cell volume is not related to the steady-state shape of the cell, it is modulated by the rate of cell shape change.
source: Our detailed characterization of cell volume during cell spreading revealed that, while cell volume is not related to the steady-state shape of the cell, it is modulated by the rate of cell shape change.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the spreading experiments.

claim: The authors propose that volume modulation during spreading is due to a coupling between cell membrane tension and rates of ion fluxes.
source: We propose that this is due to a coupling between cell membrane tension and rates of ion fluxes (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic proposal of the study.

claim: An extension of the classical PLM including mechano-osmotic coupling can account for observations of cell volume during cell spreading.
source: An extension of the classical PLM including this coupling can account for our observations of cell volume during cell spreading.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling work.

claim: Measures of membrane tension during spreading and at steady state under a variety of conditions confirmed that fast spreading is associated with a transient increase in membrane tension.
source: Measures of membrane tension during spreading and at steady state under a variety of conditions confirmed that fast spreading is associated with a transient increase in membrane tension and that preventing volume modulation leads to even higher membrane tension, as predicted by the model.
evidence: This is a summary of the tether pulling experiments.

claim: Preventing volume modulation leads to even higher membrane tension, as predicted by the model.
source: Measures of membrane tension during spreading and at steady state under a variety of conditions confirmed that fast spreading is associated with a transient increase in membrane tension and that preventing volume modulation leads to even higher membrane tension, as predicted by the model.
evidence: This is a summary of the tether pulling experiments and model predictions.

claim: The experiments and model suggest the existence of a mechano-osmotic coupling at the level of the cell membrane, which acts as a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism by reducing membrane tension changes upon fast cell deformation.
source: Taken together, these experiments and this model suggest the existence of a mechano-osmotic coupling at the level of the cell membrane, which acts as a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism by reducing membrane tension changes upon fast cell deformation (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A central hypothesis in the model is that the physical coupling between the actin cortex and the cell membrane leads to an increase in membrane tension when the rate of deformation is faster than the relaxation time of the actin cortex and membrane ensemble.
source: A central hypothesis in the model is that the physical coupling between the actin cortex and the cell membrane leads to an increase in membrane tension when the rate of deformation is faster than the relaxation time of the actin cortex and membrane ensemble.
evidence: This is a key assumption of the model.

claim: Cells treated with an inhibitor of Ezrin (20 µM NSC668394) lost less volume than control cells during spreading, despite spreading being similar or even slightly faster during the initial phase.
source: Thus, we performed an additional experiment using an inhibitor of Ezrin, membrane-cytoskeleton linker (20 µM NSC668394) and monitored cell volume during spreading. We found that while spreading was similar or even slightly faster during the initial phase, treated cells lost less volume than control cells (Figure 6A), consistent with a role of cortex/membrane coupling in mediating the effect of spreading kinetics on volume loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Electron microscopy imaging confirmed the different extent of spreading in the various conditions assayed, and the perturbation of branched actin in the CK-666 treated cells.
source: To further investigate the ultrastructure of the cell cortex during spreading, we unroofed (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019) Hela cells after 30 min spreading on a fibronectin-coated substrate. Following electron microscopy imaging confirmed the different extent of spreading in the various conditions assayed, and the perturbation of branched actin in the CK-666 treated cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Membrane folds and structures such as clathrin-coated pits and caveolae were present in all conditions.
source: Membrane folds and structures such as clathrin-coated pits and caveolae were present in all conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The sign of the volume change upon an increase in tension depends on whether the contribution of ions to the osmotic pressure increases or decreases.
source: The sign of the volume change upon an increase in tension depends on whether the contribution of ions to the osmotic pressure increases or decreases.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration from the model.

claim: An increase in sodium channel conductance upon an increase in tension leads to an increase in volume, whereas an increase in potassium conductance upon an increase in tension leads to a decrease in volume.
source: For instance, an increase in sodium channel conductance upon an increase in tension leads to an increase in volume, whereas an increase in potassium conductance upon an increase in tension leads to a decrease in volume.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: Using a detailed model of ion transport, the authors show that for physiological values of parameters, the volume is indeed expected to decrease upon an increase in tension.
source: Using a detailed model of ion transport, we show that for physiological values of parameters, as observed in experiments, the volume is indeed expected to decrease upon an increase in tension.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: For control cells, and cells treated with Y-27, EIPA, and CK-666, the effective stiffness parameter shows less than 30% variation, implying that most of the volume loss is explained by differences in spreading speed.
source: Control cells, and cells treated with Y-27, EIPA, and CK-666 show less than 30% variation in the value of ξ, implying that most of the volume loss is explained by differences in spreading speed.
evidence: This is an analysis of the model fitting parameters.

claim: For cells treated with Y-27+EIPA and Y-27+CK-666, the effective stiffness parameter decreases by an order of magnitude, leading to low volume loss even though the cells are spreading fast.
source: However, for the cells treated with Y-27+EIPA and Y-27+CK-666, ξ decreases by an order of magnitude, leading to low volume loss even though the cells are spreading fast (Appendix 1—table 4 in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an analysis of the model fitting parameters.

claim: For both Y-27+CK-666 and Y-27+EIPA, spreading is still inducing an increase in membrane tension, and the absence of volume loss reinforces the effect on membrane tension.
source: Spreading experiments show that, for both Y-27+CK-666 and Y-27+EIPA, membrane tension reaches the highest values. This means that, in both cases, spreading is still inducing an increase in membrane tension, and the absence of volume loss reinforces the effect on membrane tension.
evidence: This is an inference from the tether pulling experiments.

claim: The absence of volume loss in Y-27+CK-666 and Y-27+EIPA treated cells suggests that the elasticity parameter is not affected but rather the volume-tension electromechanical coupling.
source: It suggests that the elasticity parameter is not affected but rather the volume-tension electromechanical coupling.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting and tether pulling experiments.

claim: Branched actin networks are specifically required for the volume-tension electromechanical coupling.
source: This could mean that, unexpectedly, branched actin networks are specifically required for this coupling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the effects of CK-666 treatment.

claim: The specific requirement for branched actin could be due to a direct association of branched actin with ion channels and pumps.
source: This could be due to a direct association of branched actin with ion channels and pumps (Mazzochi et al., 2006; Shaw and Koleske, 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis with citations to previous work on actin-channel interactions.

claim: Fast imposed cell deformation induces a strong loss of volume of confined HeLa EMBL control cells, while Lat A treated cells kept a constant volume.
source: FXm volume measurement combined with confinement showed a strong loss of volume of confined HeLa EMBL control cells, while Lat A treated cells kept a constant volume (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D showing for both treatments the decrease in FXm background intensity corresponding to the confiner height; and Figure 7—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In control cells, stronger confinement led to larger volume loss, while Lat A treated cells showed no significant volume loss except for the lowest confinement height.
source: In control cells, stronger confinement led to larger volume loss, while Lat A treated cells showed no significant volume loss except for the lowest confinement height (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Treatment with Y-27632 to reduce contractility had no effect on volume loss upon confinement.
source: Conversely, treatment with Y-27632 to reduce contractility had no effect on volume loss upon confinement (Figure 7E), confirming that contractility has no direct effect on cell volume and that the effect of Y-27632 on cell volume during cell spreading is mostly via an increase of the spreading speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The loss of volume in control cells upon confinement corresponded to a deformation at an almost constant surface area.
source: The loss of volume in control cells corresponded to a deformation at an almost constant surface area (Figure 7F, calculated from the volume, see Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: This loss of volume induced by fast confinement was also found in other cell types, RPE-1 and HEK-293.
source: This loss of volume induced by fast confinement was also found in other cell types, RPE-1 and HEK-293 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G) and was also previously observed in confined Dictyostelium cells (Srivastava et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Fast imposed cell deformation induces an actin-dependent loss of volume (up to 30%), at almost constant surface area.
source: Overall, these experiments show that fast imposed cell deformation induces an actin-dependent loss of volume (up to 30%), at almost constant surface area.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the confinement experiments.

claim: The volume loss upon fast confinement occurred between two consecutive frames at 30 ms time lapse.
source: It showed that, even with a time lapse of 30 ms, the volume loss happened between two consecutive frames (Figure 7G a Figure 7—figure supplement 1H, I and Figure 7—video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-speed imaging data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Only volume is lost and not dry mass upon fast confinement.
source: Only volume is lost and not dry mass (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J), which suggests that only water and probably small solutes are lost.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The speed of volume change upon fast confinement is not compatible with the mechanosensitive PLM, as in this model, volume loss occurs in the minutes timescale due to changes in ion transport rates.
source: Nevertheless, the speed of volume change is not compatible with our mechanosensitive PLM, as in this model, volume loss occurs in the minutes timescale due to changes in ion transport rates.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the model for very fast deformations.

claim: Fast imaging showed a transient appearance of streams of darker fluid (non labeled, thus coming from the cells) emanating from confined groups of cells, likely corresponding to the expelled water and osmolites.
source: Fast imaging of the fluorescent medium surrounding the cells used for FXm indeed showed a transient appearance of streams of darker fluid (non labeled, thus coming from the cells) emanating from confined groups of cells (Figure 7H and Figure 7—video 4), likely corresponding to the expelled water and osmolites.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Although at the millisecond timescale, the mechanism of volume loss very likely differs from the context of spontaneous cell spreading, it is also induced by an increase in membrane tension, and requires the presence of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Overall, these confinement experiments suggest that, although at this timescale of milliseconds, the mechanism of volume loss very likely differs from the context of spontaneous cell spreading, it is also induced by an increase in membrane tension, and requires the presence of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the confinement experiments.

claim: The cell volume changed by a few percent as single dendritic cells moved through the collagen gel.
source: We observed that the cell volume changed by a few percent as single cells moved through the collagen gel (Figure 7I), with periods of cell protrusion corresponding to a decrease in cell volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Faster moving dendritic cells displayed larger volume fluctuations.
source: This clearly showed that faster moving cells displayed larger volume fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The relation between the coefficient of variation of the volume and the speed of migrating dendritic cells was well fitted by an extension of the model to cells moving through a meshwork.
source: Interestingly, this relation was well fitted by an extension of the model to cells moving through a meshwork (fit in Figure 7K, and see Appendix 1 for the model extension).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model fit shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The mechano-osmotic coupling is at work in migrating cells, inducing larger volume fluctuations (and thus larger density changes) in faster migrating cells.
source: This experiment suggests that the mechano-osmotic coupling that we describe in our study is at work in migrating cells, inducing larger volume fluctuations (and thus larger density changes) in faster migrating cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dendritic cell migration experiments.

claim: Volume and density fluctuations could be present in a large range of cells in physiological conditions, with yet unknown consequences on cell physiology and behavior.
source: These volume and density fluctuations could thus be present in a large range of cells in physiological conditions, with yet unknown consequences on cell physiology and behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A membrane tension homeostasis mechanism is constantly at work in mammalian cells.
source: Beyond the potential functional significance of volume and density fluctuations associated with cell shape changes, our observations and our model demonstrate that a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism is constantly at work in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The membrane tension homeostasis mechanism is most likely due to crosstalk between mechanical, osmotic, and electrical properties of the cell.
source: This mechanism is most likely due to crosstalk between mechanical, osmotic, and electrical properties of the cell pointing to the importance of taking into account complex coupling between various physical parameters to understand cellular physics and physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the nature of the mechanism.
